LazyFS

A file system that forgets data.

LazyFS keeps your writes in its own page cache and only persists what the application explicitly fsyncs. Pull the plug whenever you want and find the data-loss bugs hiding in your database — no code changes needed.

Get started ★ GitHub VLDB 2024 paper

What happens when the plug is pulled

Two ways a crash corrupts data: unsynced writes are lost, or only part of them reaches the disk. LazyFS makes both happen on demand, at the exact moment you choose.

    What your app sees (LazyFS cache)
    →
    What is really on disk (ext4)
    
        
    ⚡
    
      
    
    
    
  
    

  
  
    
    
    
      
    How it works
    
      
    
        LazyFS is a FUSE file system that sits between your system and a regular file system (e.g., ext4). Your system runs unmodified:
        just point its data directory to the LazyFS mount point. Inside LazyFS, three components decide what reaches the disk.
      
    

      
    
        

        
    
          
      
            
    • Writes stay in the LazyFS cache. Reads are served from it, so your system always sees its own data.
      • 
            
    • Data reaches ext4 only on fsync/fdatasync, or when a torn-write fault persists part of it on purpose.
      • 
            
    • A fault decides the rest. Whatever is still in the cache when a fault fires is gone, exactly what a power cut would lose.
      • 
            
    • You see what was lost. Before each fault, LazyFS logs which blocks were never persisted, so every bug comes with an explanation.
      • 
          
    
        
    
      
    
    
    
  
    

  
  
    
    
    
      
    Supported faults
    
      
    Every fault can be injected in two ways. Pick one to see the examples:
    
      
    
        
        
      
    
      
    Write a command to the FIFO while your system runs: you decide when the fault happens.
    
      
    Declare [[injection]] entries before mounting: LazyFS fires them at a precise call, e.g. “the 2nd group of writes to log.txt”.
    

      
    
        
    
          
    Lost writes
    clear
    
          
    Drops every unsynced write but keeps LazyFS running. You kill and restart your system, which is ideal for Jepsen-style tests that crash processes themselves.
    
          
    echo "lazyfs::clear-cache" > /tmp/faults.fifo
    
          
    [[injection]]
type="clear-cache"
from="/tmp/lazyfs.root/wal.log"
op="fsync"
timing="after"
occurrence=3
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Crash
    crash
    
          
    Drops unsynced data and kills LazyFS right before or after a system call on a given file. Crashing before LevelDB renames 000002.dbtmp leaves a database that cannot start (bug #3).
    
          
    echo "lazyfs::crash::timing=before::op=rename::from_rgx=dbtmp" > /tmp/faults.fifo
    
          
    [[injection]]
type="clear-cache"
from="/tmp/lazyfs.root/000002.dbtmp"
to="/tmp/lazyfs.root/CURRENT"
op="rename"
timing="before"
occurrence=1
crash=true
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Linear torn write
    torn-seq · torn-op
    
          
    Only the beginning of the data reaches the disk, e.g. the first half of a large write, or the first 2 of 4 writes. Only the first half of etcd's 16 KiB snapshot write: “invalid database” on restart (bug #16).
    
          
    echo "lazyfs::torn-op::file=/tmp/lazyfs.root/member/snap/db::persist=1::parts=2::occurrence=1" > /tmp/faults.fifo
    
          
    [[injection]]
type="torn-op"
file="/tmp/lazyfs.root/member/snap/db"
parts=2
persist=[1]
occurrence=1
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Non-linear torn write
    torn-seq · torn-op
    
          
    Later data reaches the disk without the data before it, e.g. the 4th write but not the 3rd. ZooKeeper with its 4th log write but not its 3rd: CRC error on startup (bug #8).
    
          
    echo "lazyfs::torn-seq::op=write::file=/tmp/lazyfs.root/log.txt::persist=1,4::occurrence=2" > /tmp/faults.fifo
    
          
    [[injection]]
type="torn-seq"
op="write"
file="/tmp/lazyfs.root/log.txt"
persist=[1,4]
occurrence=2
    
        
    
      
    

      
    Both torn writes can be injected on a sequence of writes to a file (torn-seq: choose which writes persist)
        or on one large write split into parts (torn-op: choose which parts persist). In both cases LazyFS crashes right after.
    

      
    
        
    Helpers
    
        
      
          
    • lazyfs::unsynced-data-report: what would be lost right now.
      • 
          
    • lazyfs::cache-checkpoint: write all unsynced data to ext4.
      • 
          
    • lazyfs::display-cache-usage: how full the cache is.
      • 
          
    • Log parser: turn on log_all_operations, then logparse/parse.py turns the log of every system call into a graph, showing where to inject faults.
      • 
        
    
        
    Full reference in the README.
    
      
    
    
    
  
    

  
  
    
    
    
      
    Get started
    
      
    Linux with FUSE 3. Tested on Debian 11 and Ubuntu 20.04 over ext4.
    

      
    
        
    
          
    1 · Build
    

    sudo apt install g++ cmake libfuse3-dev libfuse3-3 fuse3
echo "user_allow_other" | sudo tee -a /etc/fuse.conf
git clone https://github.com/dsrhaslab/lazyfs.git && cd lazyfs
cd libs/libpcache && ./build.sh && cd -
cd lazyfs && ./build.sh
    
        
    
        
    
          
    2 · Mount
    

    mkdir -p /tmp/lazyfs.mnt /tmp/lazyfs.root
./scripts/mount-lazyfs.sh -c config/default.toml \
    -m /tmp/lazyfs.mnt -r /tmp/lazyfs.root -f
    
        
    
        
    
          
    3 · Break things
    

    # what would be lost right now?
echo "lazyfs::unsynced-data-report" > /tmp/faults.fifo
# power failure: drop everything not fsynced
echo "lazyfs::clear-cache" > /tmp/faults.fifo
# crash right before an fsync to any file matching "wal"
echo "lazyfs::crash::timing=before::op=fsync::from_rgx=wal" > /tmp/faults.fifo
    
        
    
      
    
      
    
        Precise faults (torn-seq, torn-op, clear-cache) can also be
        declared in the TOML config: see Supported faults. Full reference in the
        README.
      
    
    
    
  
    

  
  
    
    
    
      
    Real bugs in real systems
    
      
    
        In our VLDB 2024 paper, we used LazyFS to reproduce 12 reported bugs (7 of them ambiguous
        reports with no reproduction steps) and to find 8 new ones, which we reported to the developers.
        Each experiment takes seconds, not hours of unplugging servers.
        Reproduce them yourself →
      
    
      
    
      
    new found with LazyFS · ✓ confirmed by the developers
    
    
    
  
    

  
  
    
    
    
      
    Used by & written about
    
      
    LazyFS runs in the test suites of production databases and has helped find data-loss bugs in systems such as NATS and ArcadeDB.
